entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To give no indication that something is going to stop, change or happen; usually said of a situation or trend that simply goes on.
entries.usage: Very common in news and conversation about weather, prices, conflicts and people's energy. It is usually followed by *of* + *-ing*, especially *slowing down, letting up, stopping* or *improving*, and both *sign* and *signs* are common. The subject is the thing that keeps going: *The strike shows no sign of ending*.
entries.pattern: show no sign(s) of + -ing / noun
examples: It's been pouring since Monday, and the rain **shows no sign of** letting up.
Despite higher interest rates, home prices **show no signs of** falling.
At 82, my grandmother **shows no sign of** slowing down; she still gardens every morning.

drill.sentence: The heat wave {{shows no sign of}} ending, so the city is keeping its cooling centers open all week.
drill.hint: no indication that it will end soon (verb + *no* + singular noun + *of*)

mistake.wrong: The rain shows no sign to stop.
mistake.right: The rain shows no sign of stopping.
mistake.why: In this phrase *sign* is followed by *of* + *-ing*, not by a *to*-infinitive.

entries.related: *there's no end in sight* — informal, usually about something unpleasant; *show signs of* — the positive form, as in *show signs of improvement*; *let up* — (of rain or pressure) become weaker.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A mistake or hidden problem that many people run into, especially when they are new to something.
entries.usage: Typical of advice articles, guides, teaching and talks, and frequent in titles such as *five common pitfalls to avoid*. The usual patterns are *a common pitfall is* + *-ing* and *one of the most common pitfalls in* + activity. It suggests a trap that is easy to fall into without noticing, so it is more vivid than *a common mistake*.
entries.pattern: a common pitfall (for / in …) is + -ing
examples: **A common pitfall** for first-time home buyers is forgetting to budget for closing costs.
When you start running, **a common pitfall** is increasing your mileage too quickly.
One **common pitfall** in data analysis is testing dozens of hypotheses and reporting only the ones that work.

drill.sentence: When you sell something online, {{a common pitfall}} is shipping the item before the payment has cleared.
drill.hint: a frequent hidden danger (not *mistake* or *trap*)

entries.related: *a common mistake* — plainer, any error; *fall into the trap of* + *-ing* — the usual verb phrase with *trap*; *a gotcha* — informal, a surprising detail that trips people up, common among programmers.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Almost all of a group, leaving only a very small minority.
entries.usage: Common in news, reports and arguments, often with figures: *the overwhelming majority of voters / cases / doctors*. After *of* + plural noun the verb is usually plural: *the overwhelming majority of residents support it*. For votes, *by an overwhelming majority* (with *an*) is the usual form.
entries.pattern: the overwhelming majority of + plural noun + plural verb
examples: We rarely charge late fees, because **the overwhelming majority** of our customers pay on time.
When our landlord surveyed the tenants, **the overwhelming majority** said they wanted better lighting in the garage.
At my son's school, kids who walk or bike make up **the overwhelming majority**.

drill.sentence: The proposal passed easily: {{the overwhelming majority}} of members voted yes, and only six voted no.
drill.hint: almost all (the adjective suggests a crushing win; not *vast*)

entries.related: *the vast majority* — very close, more frequent and slightly more neutral; *a clear majority* — comfortably more than half; *a slim majority* — only just over half.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To experience a problem or event that stops or reverses progress for a while.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports and business reports, and when talking about health, careers and projects. Adjectives often go before *setback*: *a major / serious / minor / temporary setback*. Here *suffer* simply means "experience" something bad and does not mean feeling pain; *experience a setback* and *face a setback* are plainer variants.
entries.pattern: suffer a (major / serious / temporary) setback
examples: The bridge project **suffered a major setback** when engineers found cracks in the foundation.
Her recovery **suffered a setback** when she caught pneumonia in the hospital.
The team **suffered another setback** on Sunday when its star pitcher tore a ligament in his elbow.

drill.sentence: Peace talks {{suffered a setback}} after one side walked out of the meeting on Monday.
drill.hint: progress stopped for a while (verb that often means "feel pain" + noun)

entries.related: *hit a snag* — informal, a small unexpected problem; *a step backward* — plainer, a change that undoes progress; *suffer a defeat* — lose a game, vote or battle.

entries.label: quantifier
entries.meaning: A much larger amount of something than is normal or reasonable.
entries.usage: Slightly formal but common in educated speech and writing, usually critical or humorous: the speaker thinks it is too much. Typical nouns are *time, money, attention, energy* and *paperwork*, as in *spend an inordinate amount of time on* something. With plural nouns, use *an inordinate number of*.
entries.pattern: an inordinate amount of + uncountable noun (time / money / attention)
examples: He spends **an inordinate amount of** time choosing a restaurant, then orders the same thing every time.
The new rules require **an inordinate amount of** paperwork from small family farms.
Fixing the build system has eaten up **an inordinate amount of** our time this quarter.

drill.sentence: Planning the wedding took {{an inordinate amount of}} energy, and we were exhausted before the big day.
drill.hint: unreasonably much (formal adjective; not *excessive* or *enormous*)

entries.related: *an excessive amount of* — more plainly negative; *a disproportionate amount of* — too much compared with what is fair or with others; *an ungodly amount of* — informal and humorous.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To damage something such as a plan, a hope or a cause, or to cause someone a serious disappointment.
entries.usage: A news-style phrase, very common in headlines about politics, business and sports. Adjectives are frequent, as in *a major / serious / severe / devastating blow*, and the subject is usually an event or a decision. *Deal* is irregular, so the past form is *dealt* /dɛlt/.
entries.pattern: X deals a (major / serious) blow to + plan / hopes / cause
examples: The court's decision **dealt a major blow to** the governor's plan to cut school funding.
Losing their quarterback to injury **dealt a serious blow to** the team's playoff hopes.
The closing of the paper mill **dealt a heavy blow to** the small town, which had few other jobs.

drill.sentence: Heavy rain on opening weekend {{dealt a blow to}} the festival's ticket sales.
drill.hint: seriously hurt (the verb you use for handing out playing cards + noun)

mistake.wrong: The scandal dealed a blow to his campaign.
mistake.right: The scandal dealt a blow to his campaign.
mistake.why: *Deal* is irregular: the past tense and past participle are *dealt*.

entries.related: *be a blow to* — same idea, simpler; *come as a blow* — about bad news that hurts someone; *strike a blow for* — the opposite, help a cause.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To prevent a crisis from happening, usually by acting just before it starts.
entries.usage: Common in news about politics, finance and diplomacy, often with *narrowly* or *at the last minute*; the passive *a crisis was averted* is frequent. In casual speech, *Crisis averted!* is a joking line after a small problem is solved. *Avert* means stop something that is coming, while *avoid* means keep away from something.
entries.pattern: (narrowly) avert a crisis / a crisis is averted
examples: A last-minute budget deal **averted a crisis**, so government offices will stay open.
I found my passport in the laundry basket an hour before the flight. **Crisis averted**.
Quick thinking by the nurses **averted a crisis** when the hospital's backup generator failed.

drill.sentence: The airline reached a deal with its pilots late Sunday, {{averting a crisis}} just before the holiday travel season.
drill.hint: stopping a serious emergency from happening (formal verb; not *avoiding*)

entries.related: *head off* — informal, stop something before it happens; *defuse a crisis* — calm one that has already started; *avoid* — keep away from something, a weaker idea.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: The very large amount of something, stressed as the main cause of a difficulty or of surprise.
entries.usage: *Sheer* stresses size alone: the amount itself is the problem or the impressive point. The phrase is often the subject or follows *by, because of* or *given*, as in *overwhelmed by the sheer volume of email*. With plural countable nouns, *the sheer number of* is also common.
entries.pattern: the sheer volume of + noun (email / traffic / work)
examples: After the hurricane, insurers were overwhelmed by **the sheer volume of** claims.
I love Costco, but **the sheer volume of** stuff in there makes my head spin.
Moderators struggle to keep up with **the sheer volume of** posts that get reported every day.

drill.sentence: Nobody warned us about {{the sheer volume of}} laundry a newborn produces.
drill.hint: the huge quantity of, stressing size alone (not *amount*)

entries.related: *the sheer number of* — for plural countable nouns; *the sheer scale of* — about size or extent; *the bulk of* — most of something, not its size.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make a tense or dangerous situation calmer, so that it does not turn into an argument, a fight or violence.
entries.usage: Used about arguments, protests, standoffs and workplace conflicts, often with the method: *defuse the situation with a joke* or *by apologizing*. *Defuse tension(s)* is also common. The spelling matters: *defuse* (calm; literally, remove a bomb's fuse) is different from *diffuse* (spread out), and many writers mix them up.
entries.pattern: defuse the situation (with a joke / by + -ing)
examples: When two customers started shouting at each other, the manager **defused the situation** by offering both of them a refund.
My dad has a talent for **defusing the situation** with a bad joke whenever my sisters fight.
Flight attendants are trained to **defuse situations** like this before they get out of hand.

drill.sentence: The meeting got heated, but Maria {{defused the situation}} by suggesting a ten-minute break.
drill.hint: made the tense moment calm (verb that literally means making a bomb safe)

mistake.wrong: She tried to diffuse the situation with a joke.
mistake.right: She tried to defuse the situation with a joke.
mistake.why: *Defuse* means to calm a tense situation; *diffuse* means to spread something out, such as light or heat.

entries.related: *de-escalate* — the term used by police and diplomats; *calm things down* — everyday spoken; *escalate* — the opposite, make a conflict worse.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Badly and urgently needing something, usually because a situation is serious.
entries.usage: Common in news and charity appeals: *families in dire need of food and shelter*. It usually follows *be* or a noun and can also stand without *of*, as in *people in dire need*. Used for small things, like coffee or a haircut, it sounds playfully dramatic.
entries.pattern: be in dire need of + noun
examples: After the earthquake, thousands of families are **in dire need of** clean water and shelter.
Our kitchen is **in dire need of** a makeover; the cabinets haven't changed since 1978.
Many rural hospitals are **in dire need of** nurses and doctors.

drill.sentence: I haven't slept properly in a week; I'm {{in dire need of}} a vacation.
drill.hint: urgently lacking (the adjective is not *desperate*)

entries.related: *in desperate need of* — very similar, more emotional; *badly in need of* — plainer; *could use* — casual and much milder, as in *I could use a coffee*.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make an existing problem or difficult situation worse, usually by adding a new mistake or factor.
entries.usage: Common in news, analysis and serious conversation. The subject is often a later mistake (*Lying only compounded the problem*), and the passive is frequent: *The problem was compounded by staff shortages*. Typical objects are *problem, difficulties, error, mistake* and *misery*.
entries.pattern: compound the problem / be compounded by + noun
examples: He made a mistake on his taxes, then **compounded the problem** by ignoring letters from the IRS.
Our basement was already damp, and a clogged gutter **compounded the problem**.
Hiding the dent only **compounded the problem**; my dad was angrier about the secret than about the car.

drill.sentence: Missing the first flight was bad enough, but losing my phone at the airport {{compounded the problem}}.
drill.hint: added to the difficulty (verb also used for interest that keeps growing)

entries.related: *exacerbate* — more formal, often with *pain, tension, symptoms*; *make matters worse* — everyday; *add insult to injury* — make things worse in a humiliating way.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A complete and surprising change from the usual way of doing, making or thinking about something.
entries.usage: Common in reviews, journalism and policy writing about a new style, strategy or law, as in *a radical departure from tradition*. It takes *from* unless the comparison is already clear from context, and *radical* can be replaced by *sharp, major* or *significant*. Here *departure* means a change of direction, not leaving a place.
entries.pattern: a radical departure from + previous practice / style
examples: The new library, all glass and steel, is **a radical departure from** the brick buildings around it.
The tax plan represents **a radical departure from** decades of party policy.
For a band known for loud punk songs, this quiet acoustic album is **a radical departure**.

drill.sentence: Moving from Manhattan to a farm in Vermont was {{a radical departure from}} the life she'd always known.
drill.hint: an extreme change away from (the noun literally means "leaving")

entries.related: *a break with* — similar, as in *a clean break with tradition*; *a shift* — milder and often gradual; *a return to* — the opposite, going back to an earlier style.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To control your words, feelings or actions and not react as strongly as you could, or want to.
entries.usage: Used about people in conflicts and about police, armies and governments: *Both sides were urged to show restraint*. Adjectives like *great, remarkable* and *admirable* are common, and it usually praises someone who could have overreacted. *Exercise restraint* means the same and is more formal.
entries.pattern: show (great / remarkable) restraint
examples: The referee **showed remarkable restraint** while the coach screamed at him from the sideline.
The United Nations urged both governments to **show restraint** after the border clash.
I **showed great restraint** at the bakery today and bought only one croissant.

drill.sentence: When the other driver cut him off and started yelling, Dad {{showed restraint}} and just drove on.
drill.hint: kept his reaction under control (verb + noun)

entries.related: *exercise restraint* — more formal, common in official statements; *hold back* — everyday phrasal verb; *lash out* — the opposite, react with sudden anger.

entries.label: verb + preposition + noun
entries.meaning: To continue with something, but carefully, because there may be risks or problems.
entries.usage: Common in warnings, advice and official language, and used figuratively in conversation: *I'd proceed with caution if I were you*. It is often an imperative or follows *should* or *need to*, and it sounds more serious than *be careful*. *Great* or *extreme* can strengthen it: *proceed with extreme caution*.
entries.pattern: proceed with (great / extreme) caution
examples: The roads are still icy in places, so drivers should **proceed with caution**.
If an investment sounds too good to be true, **proceed with caution**.
The results are encouraging, but doctors should **proceed with caution** until larger trials are done.

drill.sentence: My sister wants to lend her new boyfriend $10,000 for his business. I told her to {{proceed with caution}}.
drill.hint: go ahead, but carefully (formal; not *be careful*)

entries.related: *tread carefully* — figurative, about sensitive situations; *err on the side of caution* — choose the safer option; *throw caution to the wind* — the opposite, take a big risk.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To warn people publicly and urgently that something dangerous or harmful is happening.
entries.usage: Mostly figurative in news and public debate: experts, doctors or officials *sound the alarm about / on / over* a problem, which suggests that others have not noticed the danger yet. The literal sense, setting off an alarm, also exists. *Raise the alarm* is similar and more common in British English.
entries.pattern: sound the alarm about / on / over + problem
examples: Pediatricians are **sounding the alarm** about how little sleep teenagers are getting.
A junior accountant **sounded the alarm** on the fraud years before the company collapsed.
Our neighbor smelled smoke and **sounded the alarm**, so everyone got out in time.

drill.sentence: For years, public health experts have {{sounded the alarm}} about rising loneliness among older adults.
drill.hint: warned loudly and publicly (not *raised*)

entries.related: *raise the alarm* — same, more common in British English; *raise a red flag* — point out a warning sign; *blow the whistle on* — expose wrongdoing inside an organization.

entries.label: verb + object + adjective
entries.meaning: To avoid making a final choice for now, so that several possibilities stay available.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation about careers, studies, housing and dating. The possessive changes with the subject: *I'm keeping my options open*, *she wants to keep her options open*. It usually sounds sensible, but about relationships it can suggest someone who won't commit.
entries.pattern: keep my / your / their options open
examples: I haven't picked a major yet; I'm **keeping my options open**.
He says he's single, but it sounds like he's just **keeping his options open**.
The Fed is **keeping its options open** on interest rates until it sees more data.

drill.sentence: Don't sign the lease yet. You might get the job in Denver, so {{keep your options open}}.
drill.hint: don't commit to one choice yet (not *wait and see*)

entries.related: *hedge your bets* — protect yourself by backing more than one possibility; *play the field* — date several people; *commit to* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To wait until you have more information before forming or giving an opinion.
entries.usage: It sounds fair and careful, and is common when people discuss a new boss, film, policy or person: *I'll reserve judgment until I've read the whole report*. It is usually followed by *until* + clause or *on* + noun. The American spelling is *judgment*, with no *e* after the *g*.
entries.pattern: reserve judgment (on + noun / until + clause)
examples: The first episode was slow, but I'm **reserving judgment** until I've seen a few more.
Most fans are **reserving judgment** on the new coach until the season starts.
My mom met my new boyfriend once and said she'd **reserve judgment** for now.

drill.sentence: I've heard mixed things about the new restaurant, so I'll {{reserve judgment}} until I've actually eaten there.
drill.hint: wait before deciding what I think (the verb also means "book a table"; not *withhold*)

entries.related: *withhold judgment* — same, a little more formal; *give someone the benefit of the doubt* — assume the best for now; *jump to conclusions* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To replace something important that is missing or has been lost, such as a person, an activity or a service.
entries.usage: Used about personal loss (*after his wife died, volunteering filled a void*) and about markets and communities (*the new store fills a void in the neighborhood*). Common forms are *fill a void in someone's life* and *fill the void left by* someone or something. In the emotional sense it sounds a little literary.
entries.pattern: fill a void (in someone's life) / fill the void left by + noun
examples: After the kids left for college, adopting a dog **filled a void** in our lives.
When the town's only grocery store closed, a weekly farmers market **filled the void**.
Nobody can **fill the void left by** her death, but her students carry on her work.

drill.sentence: Retirement was hard at first, but teaching a pottery class has {{filled a void}} in his life.
drill.hint: replaced what was missing (the noun means "empty space"; not *gap* or *hole*)

entries.related: *fill a gap* — more practical, often about a market or a skill; *leave a void* — the cause, as in *His death left a void*; *a hole in someone's life* — informal.

entries.label: verb + adjective
entries.meaning: Of patience, to come close to running out; of a joke, excuse or idea, to become less funny, convincing or acceptable because it has been repeated too often.
entries.usage: Typical subjects are *patience, excuses, a joke, the novelty* and *someone's charm*: *My patience is wearing thin*. It is very often progressive (*is wearing thin*) or perfect (*has worn thin*), and the simple past *wore thin* is also common. The past participle is *worn*, not *weared*.
entries.pattern: patience / a joke / an excuse + is wearing thin / has worn thin
examples: I've asked them three times to turn down the music, and my patience is **wearing thin**.
His excuse about traffic **wore thin** after the fifth time he showed up late.
The novelty of working from home **wore thin** after a few months of eating lunch alone.

drill.sentence: The show's running joke was funny in season one, but by season four it had {{worn thin}}.
drill.hint: stopped being funny from overuse (not *gotten old*)

entries.related: *get old* — informal, as in *That joke is getting old*; *run out* — (of patience) end completely; *wear off* — (of an effect or a feeling) slowly disappear.

entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To go wrong, or not happen in the way that was planned.
entries.usage: A little more formal and elegant than *go wrong*, common in journalism and educated speech. Typical subjects are *plans, things* and *something*: *Something has gone badly awry*. *Awry* rhymes with *dry* (uh-RYE), and it comes after the verb, never before a noun.
entries.pattern: plans / things / something + go (badly) awry
examples: Our plan to surprise her **went awry** when she came home two hours early.
The city's switch to a new bus schedule **went awry** on day one, and thousands of commuters were late for work.
Doctors are still trying to figure out what **went awry** during the surgery.

drill.sentence: We had the whole wedding planned to the minute, but on the actual day, almost everything {{went awry}}.
drill.hint: failed to go as planned (formal adverb; not *wrong*)

mistake.why: Learners often read *awry* as AW-ree, like the start of *awful*; the stress is on the second syllable, which rhymes with *dry*.

entries.related: *go wrong* — plainer, everyday; *go haywire* — informal, especially about machines or systems; *backfire* — produce the opposite of the intended result.

entries.label: verb + object + adjective
entries.meaning: To make something no longer useful or needed, usually because something newer and better has appeared.
entries.usage: Formal and common in writing about technology, business and law. *Render* here means "make" and is followed by an object and an adjective, as in *render something useless / invalid / obsolete*; the passive *be rendered obsolete by* is frequent. In conversation, people usually say *make something obsolete*.
entries.pattern: render + object + obsolete / be rendered obsolete (by …)
examples: Streaming services have **rendered** the neighborhood video store **obsolete**.
The new law **renders** the old permits **obsolete**, so every restaurant must reapply.
Darning socks, once a basic household skill, was **rendered** almost **obsolete** by cheap clothing.

drill.sentence: Once the new bridge opened, the old ferry service was {{rendered obsolete}}.
drill.hint: made no longer needed (formal verb; not *made*)

entries.related: *make something obsolete* — the everyday version; *phase out* — remove something gradually on purpose; *outdated* — old-fashioned, but possibly still in use.

entries.label: noun + verb + adjective
entries.meaning: People in a situation feel very angry, anxious or hostile, so that an argument or conflict could easily start.
entries.usage: Common in news reports and descriptions of meetings, elections, sports rivalries and family events: *Tensions ran high at the town hall*. *Tensions* is usually plural, and *run* changes with the tense: *are running high, ran high*. *Emotions* and *feelings* can also *run high*.
entries.pattern: tensions run / are running / ran high (at / between …)
examples: **Tensions ran high** at the school board meeting as parents argued over a proposed ban on phones in class.
**Tensions have been running high** between the two neighbors ever since the new fence went up.
With the score tied in the final minute, **tensions were running high** on both benches.

drill.sentence: With my parents and my ex-husband at the same table for our daughter's graduation dinner, {{tensions ran high}}.
drill.hint: everyone was on edge, close to an argument (the verb is not *were*)

entries.related: *emotions run high* — about strong feelings of any kind; *on edge* — nervous and easily upset; *the atmosphere was tense* — a plainer description.

entries.label: verb + adjective
entries.meaning: To spread or grow quickly in a way that nobody controls, usually about something bad.
entries.usage: Used about disease, crime, corruption, rumors, misinformation and weeds, with a critical, alarmed tone: *Corruption ran rampant under the old regime*. *Rampant* can also come before a noun, as in *rampant inflation* or *rampant corruption*.
entries.pattern: rumors / fraud / disease + run rampant (in / on …)
examples: Gossip **ran rampant** in the office after the manager left without explanation.
Without regular weeding, mint will **run rampant** and take over your whole garden.
Fraud **ran rampant** in the relief program because nobody checked the applications.

drill.sentence: Every fall, colds {{run rampant}} at my kids' daycare, and somebody is always home sick.
drill.hint: spread out of control (not *run wild*)

entries.related: *run wild* — similar, also used about children and imagination; *be rife* — formal, as in *Corruption is rife*; *widespread* — neutral, without the idea of no control.

entries.label: fixed phrase
entries.meaning: To have very little time available, so you need to hurry or keep something short.
entries.usage: A polite, slightly formal way to say you are in a hurry, common at work and in service situations: *I know you're pressed for time, so I'll be brief*. It usually follows *be* or *feel* and is often softened with *a bit* or *a little*. The same pattern works with money: *pressed for cash*.
entries.pattern: be (a little / really) pressed for time
examples: I'm a little **pressed for time** this morning, so can we talk after lunch?
If you're **pressed for time**, skip the museum and just walk along the river.
Parents who are **pressed for time** often rely on frozen meals during the week.

drill.sentence: Sorry I can't stay for dessert; I'm really {{pressed for time}} tonight.
drill.hint: very short of spare minutes (a past participle that means "pushed")

entries.related: *short on time* — informal, same idea; *hard-pressed to* + verb — find it very difficult, as in *You'd be hard-pressed to find a better deal*; *strapped for cash* — informal, short of money.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To earn exactly as much money as you spend, so that you make neither a profit nor a loss.
entries.usage: Common in business, personal finance and talk about small ventures, often with *just, barely* or *finally*: *a business that barely breaks even*. It takes no object. The noun and adjective are written *break-even* or *breakeven*, as in *the break-even point*.
entries.pattern: (just / barely / finally) break even
examples: The bakery lost money for two years and finally **broke even** last spring.
After paying for gas and parking, I barely **broke even** at the flea market.
The movie cost so much to make that it needs a huge opening weekend just to **break even**.

drill.sentence: The food truck has to sell about 150 burritos a day just to {{break even}}.
drill.hint: make neither a profit nor a loss (not *cover its costs*)

entries.related: *cover your costs* — similar, plainer; *turn a profit* — make money; *in the red* / *in the black* — losing money / making money.

entries.label: verb + adjective
entries.meaning: Of a joke, speech, idea or event, to fail completely to have the intended effect, such as making people laugh or feel excited.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, reviews and journalism; typical subjects are *a joke, a speech, a plan, a campaign* and *an attempt*. It is often strengthened with *completely* and can take *with* + audience: *The ad fell flat with younger viewers*. *Fall flat on your face* is different: it describes a person failing in an embarrassing way.
entries.pattern: a joke / a speech / a plan + falls flat (with + audience)
examples: I opened my toast with a joke, but it **fell flat** and the room went quiet.
The candidate's speech on the economy **fell flat with** voters in the Midwest.
The new menu was supposed to attract younger customers, but it **fell** completely **flat**.

drill.sentence: The teacher's attempt to use slang with her students {{fell flat}}; they just rolled their eyes.
drill.hint: didn't have the effect she wanted (not *backfired*)

entries.related: *bomb* — informal American English, fail badly, especially a show or a joke; *go over well* — the opposite; *backfire* — produce the opposite of the intended effect.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To suddenly forget what you were saying or thinking about, usually because something interrupted you.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, meetings and talks, often as a quick apology: *Sorry, I've lost my train of thought*. The possessive changes with the subject (*he lost his train of thought*). It is often followed by *Where was I?*, which asks the listeners to remind you.
entries.pattern: lose my / your / his train of thought
examples: The fire alarm went off and I **lost my train of thought**. Where was I?
Halfway through her answer, the senator **lost her train of thought** and paused for several seconds.
Every time the baby cries, I **lose my train of thought** and have to start the paragraph over.

drill.sentence: The doorbell rang in the middle of my story, and I completely {{lost my train of thought}}.
drill.hint: suddenly had no idea what I'd been about to say (not *the thread*)

entries.related: *lose the thread* — same idea, also about following a story or argument; *my mind went blank* — forget everything, often from stress; *get sidetracked* — drift to a different topic.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To agree with or hold a particular opinion, often one that other people dispute.
entries.usage: Formal and common in academic writing, opinion pieces and careful discussion; it presents an opinion as one position among several. The pattern is *subscribe to the view / idea / theory that*, and it is often negative: *I don't subscribe to the view that…*. In casual speech, *I don't buy that* is more natural.
entries.pattern: (don't) subscribe to the view / idea that + clause
examples: Many economists **subscribe to the view that** small, regular rate increases are safer than sudden ones.
I don't **subscribe to the view that** kids need a phone to fit in at school.
The coach **subscribes to the view that** defense wins championships.

drill.sentence: My grandmother firmly {{subscribes to the view that}} a good breakfast solves most problems.
drill.hint: believes in the idea (verb also used for magazines; not *holds*)

mistake.wrong: I don't subscribe the view that money buys happiness.
mistake.right: I don't subscribe to the view that money buys happiness.
mistake.why: In this sense *subscribe* always needs *to*, just as in *subscribe to a newsletter*.

entries.related: *hold the view that* — similar, a little more neutral; *buy* — informal, as in *I don't buy that*; *take the view that* — formal, often for an official position.

entries.label: verb + preposition + noun
entries.meaning: To seem much less important, serious, impressive or good when compared with something else.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, reviews and journalism. The pattern is *A pales in comparison to / with B*, and *to* is more frequent in American English; *pale by comparison* is also common. It is often used to put problems in perspective: *My worries pale in comparison*.
entries.pattern: A pales in comparison to / with B
examples: My forty-minute commute **pales in comparison to** my sister's two hours each way.
The sequel is fun, but it **pales in comparison to** the original.
The damage from last year's storm **pales in comparison to** what this hurricane did.

drill.sentence: Their tiny apartment in Brooklyn {{pales in comparison to}} the house they had in Ohio, but they love the city.
drill.hint: looks much less impressive next to (not *is nothing compared*)

entries.related: *be nothing compared to* — informal and stronger; *pale beside* — more literary; *outshine* — the active view, be much better than.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make people trust or believe someone less, often gradually.
entries.usage: Common in politics, law, journalism and work; the subject is often a mistake, a lie or an opponent, as in *The scandal undermined her credibility with voters*. *Undermine the credibility of* + report, study or witness is also frequent. *Seriously* and *badly* often go before *undermine*.
entries.pattern: undermine someone's credibility (with + group)
examples: One false statement under oath can **undermine a witness's credibility** with the jury.
Constantly overpromising will **undermine your credibility** with clients.
Parents who threaten punishments and never follow through **undermine their own credibility**.

drill.sentence: The coach kept making promises he couldn't keep, which {{undermined his credibility}} with the players.
drill.hint: made people trust him less (formal verb; not *hurt* or *damaged*)

entries.related: *damage someone's reputation* — broader, about what people think of you; *lose face* — be embarrassed in public; *bolster someone's credibility* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To value something especially highly and treat it as more important than other things.
entries.usage: Neutral to formal, common in business, education and journalism: *The company places a premium on loyalty*. *Put a premium on* means the same and is a little more casual. The object is usually a quality or skill, such as *speed, privacy, experience* or *punctuality*.
entries.pattern: place / put a premium on + quality
examples: Our coach **places a premium on** effort, so anyone who skips practice doesn't start.
Buyers in this neighborhood **place a premium on** good schools, so prices are high.
Startups tend to **place a premium on** speed, sometimes at the expense of quality.

drill.sentence: My grandparents {{placed a premium on}} education and saved for years to send all six kids to college.
drill.hint: valued especially highly (the verb is not *put*)

entries.related: *prioritize* — put first in order; *value* — plainer, without the idea of ranking; *place little value on* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To go beyond the usual limits of what is accepted, allowed or thought possible.
entries.usage: Usually positive about art, science, sport and design (*push the boundaries of what's possible*), but about children or behavior it means testing the rules: *Toddlers push boundaries all day*. It is used with or without *the*. *Push the envelope* is similar and more informal.
entries.pattern: push the boundaries of + field / what is possible
examples: The chef likes to **push the boundaries** of traditional Mexican cooking.
Teenagers naturally **push boundaries**, so set clear rules and stick to them.
The new telescope **pushes the boundaries** of what astronomers can see.

drill.sentence: Her fashion designs {{push the boundaries}} of what people think a business suit can look like.
drill.hint: go beyond the accepted limits (not *the envelope*)

entries.related: *push the envelope* — similar, more informal, from aviation; *break new ground* — do something new; *play it safe* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A relationship in which one thing directly causes another, not just a pattern of the two appearing together.
entries.usage: Common in science, medicine, law and news about studies: *establish / prove / find a causal link between A and B*. It is often contrasted with a *correlation* or an *association*. Watch the spelling: *causal* (about causes) is easy to confuse with *casual* (relaxed).
entries.pattern: establish / prove a causal link between A and B
examples: Scientists have established **a causal link** between smoking and lung cancer.
My dad is convinced there's **a causal link** between rainy weather and his knee pain.
The lawsuit failed because the family couldn't prove **a causal link** between the drug and his illness.

drill.sentence: Ice cream sales and shark attacks both rise in summer, but there's no {{causal link}} between them.
drill.hint: relationship in which one makes the other happen (adjective + noun; not *direct*)

mistake.wrong: There is no casual link between the two events.
mistake.right: There is no causal link between the two events.
mistake.why: *Causal* means "related to a cause"; *casual* means "relaxed", and the two are often mixed up in writing.

entries.related: *a correlation* — the two things change together, without proof of cause; *a causal relationship* — same, more formal; *a connection* — vague, any kind of link.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To bring people with different views to general agreement, usually through discussion and compromise.
entries.usage: Common in politics, management and community work: *build consensus around a plan*, *build consensus among members*. It suggests patient effort rather than giving orders. *Reach (a) consensus* is the result, while *build consensus* is the process.
entries.pattern: build consensus (on / around + plan; among + group)
examples: The new mayor spent months **building consensus** for the bike lanes before the vote.
A good manager **builds consensus** before announcing a big change, not after.
With six siblings, **building consensus** on where to spend Thanksgiving is a project in itself.

drill.sentence: Before the homeowners association voted on the new pool rules, the board met with residents to {{build consensus}}.
drill.hint: slowly bring everyone toward agreement (the process; not *reach*)

entries.related: *reach a consensus* — the result of the process; *get everyone on board* — informal; *impose a decision* — the opposite approach.

entries.label: verb + preposition + noun
entries.meaning: To face opposition from people when you try to do, introduce or change something.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and history writing; the subject is usually a plan, proposal or policy, or the person behind it: *The plan met with strong resistance from teachers*. Adjectives like *strong, fierce, stiff* and *little* are frequent, and *from* introduces the opponents. *Meet resistance* without *with* is also correct.
entries.pattern: meet with (strong / fierce) resistance from + group
examples: The plan to close two neighborhood schools **met with fierce resistance** from parents.
When I tried to buckle my toddler into his car seat, I **met with** loud **resistance**.
The company's return-to-office policy **met with resistance** from employees who had moved out of the city.

drill.sentence: The proposal to raise bus fares {{met with resistance}} from riders and several city council members.
drill.hint: was strongly opposed (verb + *with* + noun; not *opposition*)

entries.related: *meet with opposition* — very similar; *face pushback* — informal, common at work; *meet with approval* — the opposite, with the same verb.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To formally ask someone to explain something more clearly because it is unclear or confusing.
entries.usage: Formal and typical of emails, official letters, law and workplace communication: *seek clarification on / about* a point, *seek clarification from* a person or office. In conversation people usually *ask for clarification* or just say *Could you clarify that?* The past form is *sought*.
entries.pattern: seek clarification on / about + point (from + person)
examples: I'm writing to **seek clarification** on the new parking rules for residents.
The defense attorney **sought clarification** from the judge about the jury instructions.
Several airlines have **sought clarification** from regulators about the new rules for carrying batteries.

drill.sentence: Before signing the lease, we {{sought clarification}} from the landlord about who pays for repairs.
drill.hint: formally asked for a clearer explanation (not *asked for*)

mistake.why: *Seek* is irregular: the past tense and past participle are *sought* /sɔt/.

entries.related: *ask for clarification* — the everyday version; *request clarification* — equally formal, common in official letters; *clear up* — informal, resolve a confusion.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make people consider that something might be true or might happen, without claiming that it is.
entries.usage: Common in news, reports and analysis; the subject is often evidence, a finding or an event, but it can be a person. It takes a *that* clause, or *of* + noun or *-ing*, as in *raise the possibility of a strike*. It sounds neutral and careful, unlike *claim*.
entries.pattern: raise the possibility that + clause / of + noun
examples: The doctor **raised the possibility that** my headaches are caused by my new glasses.
The construction delays **raise the possibility that** the stadium won't be ready for opening day.
New satellite images **raise the possibility that** the glacier is melting faster than expected.

drill.sentence: His lawyer {{raised the possibility that}} the security camera had recorded the wrong date.
drill.hint: made people consider (verb + noun + *that*; not *suggested*)

entries.related: *suggest* — plainer and shorter; *open up the possibility that* — make something possible for the first time; *rule out the possibility* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Permission that a person gives for a treatment, procedure or study after its risks, benefits and alternatives have been fully explained.
entries.usage: A technical term in medicine, research ethics and law. Typical verbs are *give, obtain* and *get*, and patients *sign an informed consent form*. It is also used more loosely about privacy and data, for example when users agree to tracking without understanding it.
entries.pattern: give / obtain informed consent (for + procedure)
examples: Before the surgery, the doctor explained the risks and asked me to sign an **informed consent** form.
All participants gave **informed consent** before the study began.
The hospital was sued for operating without the patient's **informed consent**.

drill.sentence: A patient who doesn't understand the risks hasn't truly given {{informed consent}}.
drill.hint: permission given after the risks are explained (two words)

entries.related: *consent* — permission in general; *opt in* — actively choose to take part; *waiver* — a signed document that gives up a right or claim.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A very clear and complete success that nobody can doubt.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and speeches about events, campaigns, launches and performances; it sounds enthusiastic and a little formal. *Resounding* also goes with *victory, defeat, yes* and *no*: *The answer was a resounding no*. In conversation people also say *a huge success* or *a big hit*.
entries.pattern: be / prove (to be) a resounding success
examples: The bake sale was **a resounding success**: we sold out in an hour and raised $2,000 for the library.
Critics called the Broadway revival **a resounding success**.
By most measures, the city's new bike-share program has been **a resounding success**.

drill.sentence: Our first family reunion in twenty years was {{a resounding success}}; everyone wants to do it again next summer.
drill.hint: a total, clear triumph (the adjective also describes a loud echo; not *huge*)

entries.related: *a huge success* — everyday, less formal; *a smash hit* — informal, a very popular show, song or product; *a resounding failure* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Increasing agreement among a group of people, especially experts, that something is true or should be done.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, academic writing and policy debate, typically *There is a growing consensus that…* or *a growing consensus among doctors*. It suggests that an opinion is spreading but is not yet universal. Avoid *consensus of opinion*, which many editors consider redundant.
entries.pattern: there is a growing consensus (among + group) that + clause
examples: There's **a growing consensus** among my friends that brunch is overpriced.
**A growing consensus** has emerged in the league that the playoff format needs to change.
Despite **a growing consensus** among researchers that the drug works, regulators haven't approved it yet.

drill.sentence: The city council is responding to {{a growing consensus}} that the old stadium should be torn down.
drill.hint: more and more agreement (the adjective is an *-ing* form; not *general*)

entries.related: *a broad consensus* — wide agreement already in place; *a shift in opinion* — change without agreement yet; *opinion is divided* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: An event or fact that makes people remember, clearly and unpleasantly, something serious such as a danger or a problem.
entries.usage: Very common in news and speeches after accidents, disasters and crimes. The patterns are *a stark reminder of* + noun and *a stark reminder that* + clause, often after *serve as*. The tone is serious, so about small everyday things it sounds humorous.
entries.pattern: (serve as) a stark reminder of + noun / that + clause
examples: The wildfire was **a stark reminder** of how quickly a dry summer can turn dangerous.
My cholesterol results were **a stark reminder** that I can't eat like I'm twenty anymore.
The empty storefronts on Main Street serve as **a stark reminder** of what the factory closure did to the town.

drill.sentence: The near miss on the highway was {{a stark reminder}} that texting while driving can kill.
drill.hint: a clear and serious warning (the adjective also means "bare"; not *grim* or *sobering*)

entries.related: *a sobering reminder* — makes you serious and thoughtful; *a timely reminder* — comes at a useful moment; *a wake-up call* — informal, a warning that makes you change.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To formally accept that something is your duty or that you are in charge of it.
entries.usage: Formal and common in business, law and official announcements: *She will assume responsibility for the European division in March*. It can also mean accepting blame, but *take responsibility for* is more usual for blame and in conversation. *Assume* here means "take on", not "suppose".
entries.pattern: assume (full) responsibility for + noun / -ing
examples: After the merger, Lisa will **assume responsibility for** all customer support teams.
When his father got sick, the eldest son **assumed responsibility for** running the family farm.
Under the new agreement, the city **assumes responsibility for** maintaining the park.

drill.sentence: After the coach quit midseason, two of the parents {{assumed responsibility for}} running practices.
drill.hint: formally took on the duty of (the verb also means "suppose"; not *took*)

entries.related: *take responsibility for* — more common, especially for admitting blame; *take charge of* — start leading or controlling; *shirk responsibility* — the opposite, avoid a duty.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To decide which topics or problems will be discussed or treated as important, at a meeting or more broadly in a group or society.
entries.usage: Used literally about meetings and very often figuratively about politics and the media: *Social media now sets the agenda for news coverage*. It implies power, because whoever sets the agenda controls what others focus on. It often takes *for* + event or group.
entries.pattern: set the agenda (for + meeting / debate)
examples: The chair **sets the agenda** for each board meeting and sends it out a week ahead.
The league's new commissioner quickly **set the agenda**: shorter games and fewer TV timeouts.
For decades, a few big newspapers **set the agenda** for national political debate.

drill.sentence: My mother-in-law likes to {{set the agenda}} for every holiday, down to what time we eat.
drill.hint: decide what gets planned and discussed (not *call the shots*)

entries.related: *call the shots* — informal, make the important decisions; *drive the conversation* — strongly influence what people talk about; *follow someone's lead* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Change that happens slowly through a series of small steps rather than all at once.
entries.usage: Common in politics, business and management writing, often contrasted with *radical, sweeping* or *transformative change*. It can sound positive (realistic, safe) or critical (too slow): *Voters are tired of incremental change*. Both *incremental change* and the plural *incremental changes* are common.
entries.pattern: make incremental changes / bring about incremental change
examples: Activists argue that **incremental change** won't solve the housing crisis.
I lost twenty pounds through **incremental changes**, like walking after dinner and cutting out soda.
Critics say the company's new phones offer only **incremental changes**, not real innovation.

drill.sentence: Instead of renovating the whole house at once, they made {{incremental changes}} over ten years.
drill.hint: step-by-step improvements (the adjective is not *gradual* or *small*)

entries.related: *gradual change* — plainer, very close; *sweeping change* — large and fast, the opposite; *baby steps* — informal, very small steps.

entries.label: verb + preposition + noun
entries.meaning: Of a law, rule or agreement, to officially start to apply.
entries.usage: Common in news, legal texts and workplace announcements, usually with a date or time: *The ban comes into effect at midnight*. In American English, *take effect* and *go into effect* are more frequent, but *come into effect* is also used. The subject is a law, rule, change or agreement.
entries.pattern: a law / rule / ban + comes into effect (on + date)
examples: The new parking rules **come into effect** next month, so you'll need a permit to park on our street.
The ceasefire was due to **come into effect** at midnight, but the fighting continued.
Once the new policy **comes into effect**, employees will get twelve weeks of paid parental leave.

drill.sentence: The tax increase was passed in March but won't {{come into effect}} until next year.
drill.hint: officially start to apply (the verb is not *take* or *go*)

entries.related: *take effect* — the same, very common in American English; *go into effect* — also common in American news; *be repealed* — the opposite, officially canceled.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: An effect that causes harm or damage to something.
entries.usage: Formal and typical of reports, academic writing, health advice and official statements, almost always as *have a detrimental effect on* something. In conversation, people more often say *a bad effect* or simply *hurt*. *Be detrimental to* is the related adjective pattern.
entries.pattern: have a detrimental effect on + noun
examples: Lack of sleep can have **a detrimental effect** on your mood and concentration.
The new mall's **detrimental effect** on downtown businesses was obvious within a year.
Adding more layers had **a detrimental effect** on the model's accuracy.

drill.sentence: Years of loud concerts had {{a detrimental effect}} on his hearing.
drill.hint: a harmful influence (formal adjective; not *negative*, *harmful* or *damaging*)

mistake.wrong: Stress has a detrimental effect to your immune system.
mistake.right: Stress has a detrimental effect on your immune system.
mistake.why: *Effect* takes *on*; *to* belongs to the adjective pattern *be detrimental to*.

entries.related: *an adverse effect* — formal, common in medicine; *a negative impact* — common in business writing; *a beneficial effect* — the opposite.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Strongly determined to do things yourself and make your own decisions, without help or control from others.
entries.usage: Usually admiring, but it can suggest stubbornness, especially about older relatives who refuse help. It describes people and also newspapers, towns or institutions that resist outside control. It follows *be* or comes before a noun, as in *a fiercely independent woman*.
entries.pattern: be fiercely independent / a fiercely independent + noun
examples: She's **fiercely independent** and moved across the country alone at nineteen.
The paper has stayed **fiercely independent**, refusing money from any political party.
The town is **fiercely independent** and has twice voted against merging with the city next door.

drill.sentence: At ninety, Uncle Joe is still {{fiercely independent}} and gets annoyed if anyone tries to carry his groceries.
drill.hint: extremely self-reliant (the adverb also means "aggressively"; not *stubbornly* or *very*)

entries.related: *self-reliant* — neutral, depends on yourself; *stubborn* — negative, refuses to change; *clingy* — informal, the opposite, too dependent on others.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: An idea, topic or problem that appears again and again in a work, a conversation or a series of events.
entries.usage: Common in reviews, literary analysis, journalism and meeting summaries: *Family is a recurring theme in her novels*. *Recurring* also goes with *problem, dream, role* and *character*. Note the spelling *recurring*, with a double *r*; *reoccurring* exists but is far less common in this phrase.
entries.pattern: a recurring theme in + work / conversation
examples: Grief is **a recurring theme** in his songs, especially on the last two albums.
Money was **a recurring theme** in almost every argument my parents had.
**A recurring theme** in the customer complaints was slow delivery.

drill.sentence: His difficult childhood is {{a recurring theme}} in almost every interview he gives.
drill.hint: a topic that keeps coming back (not *running*, *common* or *constant*)

entries.related: *a common thread* — something shared by several different things; *a leitmotif* — formal, a repeated theme in music or literature; *a one-off* — the opposite, something that happens once.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A crisis that has fully developed into its most serious form, often after starting as a smaller problem.
entries.usage: Common in news and serious conversation, often with *turn into, become* or *escalate into*: *The dispute escalated into a full-blown crisis*. *Full-blown* also goes with *war, recession, panic* and *scandal*, and it is hyphenated before a noun. About small problems, it sounds dramatic or joking.
entries.pattern: turn / escalate into a full-blown crisis
examples: What started as a minor billing error turned into **a full-blown crisis** for the company.
By August, the water shortage had turned into **a full-blown crisis** for local farmers.
Running out of diapers at midnight felt like **a full-blown crisis** to us as new parents.

drill.sentence: If the two countries don't reopen talks soon, the trade dispute could become {{a full-blown crisis}}.
drill.hint: a fully developed emergency (not *major* or *real*)

entries.related: *a full-scale crisis* — the same idea; *a looming crisis* — one that is about to happen; *a minor hiccup* — informal, the opposite, a small problem.

entries.label: noun + of + noun
entries.meaning: The duty to prove that a claim is true; it falls on the person who makes the claim or brings the case.
entries.usage: A legal term (*the burden of proof lies with the state*) that is also very common in debates and everyday arguments. Typical patterns are *the burden of proof is on / lies with / falls on* someone, and *shift the burden of proof* to someone else.
entries.pattern: the burden of proof is on / lies with + person
examples: In a criminal trial, **the burden of proof** is on the prosecution, not the defendant.
In any argument, **the burden of proof** should fall on the person making the claim.
Some lawmakers want to shift **the burden of proof** to companies, so they must show their products are safe.

drill.sentence: My brother claims he saw a bear in our backyard, but {{the burden of proof}} is on him: I want a photo.
drill.hint: the duty to show the claim is true (not *onus*)

entries.related: *the onus* — formal, the responsibility, as in *The onus is on you*; *beyond a reasonable doubt* — the standard of proof in US criminal trials; *prove someone wrong* — show that a claim is false.
